title: 2 Chronicles 32:20–23
context: Chronicles reports the response to Assyria in brief: Hezekiah the king and Isaiah the prophet, the son of Amoz, pray and cry to heaven. In 2 Kings 19 Hezekiah prays in the temple and Isaiah sends the LORD’s answer, while here both are said to pray. The LORD sends an angel who cuts off the mighty men, leaders, and captains in the Assyrian camp, without the number given in 2 Kings 19:35, and Sennacherib returns home in shame, where in the house of his god those who came out of his own body kill him with the sword; 2 Kings 19:37 names Adrammelech and Sharezer without that description. The LORD saves Jerusalem and guides it on every side, and many bring gifts to the LORD and to Hezekiah. Arminian and Reformed readers commonly treat the passage as shared ground about prayer in crisis, the LORD’s deliverance, and his humbling of the proud.

verses.text: Hezekiah the king and Isaiah the prophet, the son of Amoz, prayed because of this, and cried to heaven.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Hezekiah the king and Isaiah the prophet praying and crying to heaven. In crisis, leaders turn to prayer.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see their prayer as the appointed means through which God acts, consistent with the fuller prayer in 2 Kings 19:15–19. Both traditions commonly read the verse as a model of crying to God in distress.

verses.text: The LORD sent an angel, who cut off all the mighty men of valor, the leaders, and captains in the camp of the king of Assyria. So he returned with shame of face to his own land. When he had come into the house of his god, those who came out of his own body killed him there with the sword.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD sending an angel to cut off the Assyrian leaders, and Sennacherib returning in shame, where those who came out of his own body killed him in his god’s house. God humbles the proud.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the deliverance and the king’s end as the LORD’s judgment on blasphemy, reported briefly here. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse soberly, as the text presents it, without speculating about how it happened.

verses.text: Thus the LORD saved Hezekiah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem from the hand of Sennacherib the king of Assyria and from the hand of all others, and guided them on every side.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD saving Hezekiah and Jerusalem and guiding them on every side. Deliverance is God’s work from first to last.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as affirming God’s faithfulness to his people (compare Psalm 46:7). Both traditions commonly read it as a celebration of the LORD’s saving power.

verses.text: Many brought gifts to the LORD to Jerusalem, and precious things to Hezekiah king of Judah, so that he was exalted in the sight of all nations from then on.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see many bringing gifts to the LORD and precious things to Hezekiah, so that he was exalted among the nations. God’s deliverance draws recognition.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the honor given to Hezekiah as flowing from what God had done. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as setting the stage for the test of pride that follows.
